text: Honest answer: today nothing routes it, and the design hasn't settled how. There's also no 'face.spirit' host to reach: the face isn't a hostname, it's the process Caddy hands the request to (puppetPost on the VPS). What has to happen: DNS sends join.spirit.andyflinn.com to the VPS; Caddy there ends TLS for that name and forwards to puppetPost's loopback port, keeping the Host header; puppetPost hands appFaceApp {host: 'join.spirit.andyflinn.com', path: '/'}; appFaceApp forwards it to your node (appServerPost), and join answers with its page. Two ways to make the first two steps work: (a) ONE PER NAME, as the relays do today (bash/tls: a site file per domain, plus a DNS record). Simple, but every grant, yours or Alice's, means editing DNS and Caddy by hand. (b) WILDCARD, RECOMMENDED: one DNS record *.spirit.andyflinn.com to the VPS, and one Caddy block for *.spirit.andyflinn.com with on-demand TLS. Before Caddy fetches a certificate for a new name it asks puppetPost 'is this name granted?', and only granted names get one. A new grant then works with nothing touched, and a random name gets no certificate. It matches your 'one face-allotment for all apps, even member apps'. Go! = (b), which becomes a G17 slice: the 'is it granted' check on puppetPost, plus the Caddy block in bash/.

Yes, Caddy does it, and my ask just above spells it out. The only 'trick' is Caddy's on-demand TLS asking puppetPost whether a name is granted before it takes on that name. The rest is plain forwarding.

It can, through the owner door: your node sends the puppet a command, and the puppet writes a Caddy site file and reloads Caddy (or calls Caddy's admin API on the VPS's loopback). But (b) gets you the same result without it, and more safely. With the wildcard block, your grant table IS what Caddy consults: before taking on a name, Caddy asks 'is this granted?', and the answer comes from your grants. So a new grant is live with nothing pushed, and a revoked one stops at its next certificate. Remote configuration costs two things (b) doesn't: a process on the VPS that may rewrite Caddy's config, so a compromised puppet could route any domain anywhere; and a DNS record per name anyway, unless DNS is wildcard too. So I'd keep remote configuration as the fallback, in case on-demand TLS ever turns out not to suit, and go with (b).

Yes, and with (b) it's small, because nothing has to be copied or kept in sync. There's no site file per name to maintain: one wildcard block, and Caddy asks before taking on each new name. The mechanism, end to end: (1) Caddy's on-demand TLS 'ask' points at puppetPost on the VPS's loopback: GET /granted?domain=join.spirit.andyflinn.com. (2) puppetPost hands that to appFaceApp (the VPS copy), which holds no table, so it asks the one that does: an appFaceApp packet to your node, { verb: 'granted?', name: 'join' }. That's the grant exchange's own app protocol, one more question beside 'grant', not a node verb. (3) Your node's appFaceApp answers from grants.json: yes plus the grantee's key, or no. (4) The VPS answers Caddy 200 or 404, and remembers a yes for a while (say an hour) so a restart doesn't re-ask for every name. Caddy only asks when it needs a certificate, which is rare, so the round trip to your node costs nothing that matters. Your table stays the only copy, which is your 'A name grant persists ... but only on the owners node'. Go! = I write this into G17 as its next slice, with the pending checks declared, before any code.

Correction, thanks to wsl-claude: you already ruled this, and my 'ask' mechanism isn't needed. PUPPETS.md §10 (:197-201): one wildcard certificate, '*.spirit.<domain>', with a flat namespace. So Caddy gets ONE block, '*.spirit.andyflinn.com { reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:<face port> }', with the wildcard certificate, and knows nothing about grants. Every subdomain lands on puppetPost with its host; appFaceApp forwards it to your node; your node looks the host up in grants.json and routes it, or refuses by name when there's no row. Nothing is slaved, pushed or configured per name: your table is the only place routes live, as before. The one cost: a wildcard certificate needs a DNS challenge, so the VPS's Caddy holds an API token for your DNS provider. My on-demand option avoided that token, but it would be a second mechanism beside your ruling. Go! = the ruled wildcard: I write the Caddy block and the no-row refusal into G17 as its next slice. Which DNS provider holds andyflinn.com? That decides the Caddy DNS module.

Right, and thanks. §10 already ruled the wildcard certificate. I've corrected myself to Andy (a single block with a DNS challenge, the no-row refusal in the owner-side lookup) and asked which DNS provider holds andyflinn.com, since that picks the Caddy DNS module.

Two readings, both workable. (1) The app IS the parent: e.g. join is served at spirit.andyflinn.com itself, with members at *.spirit.andyflinn.com. Fine and cheap. A wildcard certificate doesn't cover its own parent, so Caddy's one block names both, 'spirit.andyflinn.com, *.spirit.andyflinn.com', and fetches two certificates, which is normal. Routing doesn't change: the bare host gets a row in grants.json like any other name. (2) Each app becomes a parent with its own layer below, e.g. *.join.spirit.andyflinn.com for join's members. That's a second wildcard level, and a wildcard covers exactly one label, so it costs one more wildcard certificate per app that has its own members. §10 chose the flat namespace for exactly that reason, and you put 'wildcard levels of subdomains' out of scope for now. It's not blocked, just a certificate per level when you want it. Which one did you mean?

Yes, exactly. One Caddy block, 'app.spirit.andyflinn.com, *.app.spirit.andyflinn.com { reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:<face port> }', sends the parent and every name under it to the same place, puppetPost. Caddy keeps the Host header, so 'alice.app.spirit.andyflinn.com' arrives as that host, and the decision stays where it belongs: appFaceApp forwards to your node, and your grants.json says whose it is, or refuses by name. Caddy only terminates TLS and forwards. Certificates: one ordinary one for app.spirit.andyflinn.com and one wildcard for *.app.spirit.andyflinn.com (DNS challenge). If that's the shape you want, it replaces the flat *.spirit layer in §10 for this app, one level down. Say so and I record it as your ruling, superseding §10's flat namespace.
